stem: The Revolt of 1857 began among the sepoys at which cantonment on 10 May 1857?
solution: The mutiny broke out at Meerut on 10 May 1857, from where the sepoys marched to Delhi.

stem: The immediate spark for the revolt was the introduction of the new Enfield rifle, whose cartridges were believed to be greased with:
options: The fat of cows and pigs
solution: Sepoys believed the cartridges were greased with cow and pig fat — offensive to both Hindus and Muslims — as they had to bite them open.

stem: The sepoy who attacked his officers at Barrackpore on 29 March 1857 and became an early martyr of the revolt was:
solution: Mangal Pandey of the 34th Native Infantry rebelled at Barrackpore on 29 March 1857 and was hanged on 8 April 1857.

stem: Mangal Pandey was executed (hanged) on:
solution: Mangal Pandey was hanged on 8 April 1857, shortly after his act of defiance at Barrackpore.

stem: After capturing Delhi, the rebels proclaimed which person as their leader/emperor?
solution: The rebel sepoys proclaimed the last Mughal emperor, Bahadur Shah Zafar, as their symbolic leader.

stem: The rebellion at Kanpur was led by:
solution: Nana Saheb, the adopted son of the late Peshwa Baji Rao II, led the revolt at Kanpur.

stem: Nana Saheb was the adopted son of which former ruler?
solution: Nana Saheb was the adopted son of Peshwa Baji Rao II; the British had refused him his father's pension, fuelling his rebellion.

stem: The revolt at Jhansi was led by:
solution: Rani Lakshmibai led the revolt at Jhansi, fighting valiantly against the British.

stem: The leader of the revolt at Lucknow (Awadh) was:
solution: Begum Hazrat Mahal led the uprising in Lucknow, proclaiming her son Birjis Qadr as ruler of Awadh.

stem: Kunwar Singh, an aged leader of the revolt, belonged to which region?
solution: Kunwar Singh, a zamindar of Jagdishpur (Arrah) in Bihar, was a prominent leader of the 1857 revolt despite his old age.

stem: The able military commander who led the rebel forces in Delhi was:
solution: General Bakht Khan took charge of the rebel military organisation in Delhi under the nominal leadership of Bahadur Shah Zafar.

stem: The close associate of Nana Saheb who continued guerrilla resistance and was executed in 1859 was:
solution: Tantia Tope, an aide of Nana Saheb, carried on the fight after major defeats and was captured and executed in 1859.

stem: Rani Lakshmibai of Jhansi died fighting in:
solution: Rani Lakshmibai died in battle near Gwalior in June 1858.

stem: The leader of the revolt in the Faizabad region, a religious figure, was:
solution: Maulvi Ahmadullah Shah was an important leader of the revolt in the Awadh/Faizabad region.

stem: One major political cause of the revolt was the British policy of annexing states, especially the:
options: Doctrine of Lapse and the annexation of Awadh (1856)
solution: Annexations under the Doctrine of Lapse and the takeover of Awadh in 1856 caused deep resentment among rulers and people alike.

stem: Awadh, whose annexation in 1856 angered many, had been taken over on the grounds of:
solution: Awadh was annexed in 1856 on the pretext of 'misgovernment', deeply offending its ruler Wajid Ali Shah and the people of Awadh.

stem: A social/religious cause of the revolt was the fear among Indians that the British intended to:
options: Convert them to Christianity and interfere with their religion and customs
solution: Missionary activity and social reforms bred a fear that the British aimed to destroy Indian religions and convert people to Christianity.

stem: The British recaptured Delhi from the rebels in:
solution: British forces retook Delhi in September 1857 after fierce fighting.

stem: After the fall of Delhi, Bahadur Shah Zafar was tried and exiled to:
solution: Bahadur Shah Zafar was captured, tried, and exiled to Rangoon (present-day Yangon, Myanmar), where he died in 1862.

stem: Bahadur Shah Zafar, the last Mughal emperor, died in exile in:
solution: Bahadur Shah Zafar died in Rangoon in 1862, marking the formal end of the Mughal dynasty.

stem: As a direct result of the revolt, the British Crown took over the governance of India from the East India Company through the:
solution: The Government of India Act 1858 ended Company rule and transferred power over India to the British Crown.

stem: Under the post-1858 arrangement, the Governor-General of India was also given the new title of:
solution: The Governor-General now also served as the Viceroy, representing the British Crown in India.

stem: The first Viceroy of India was:
solution: Lord Canning, who was Governor-General during the revolt, became the first Viceroy of India after 1858.

stem: A new office created in Britain in 1858 to manage Indian affairs was that of the:
solution: The post of Secretary of State for India, assisted by the India Council, was created in Britain to oversee the administration of India.

stem: After 1858, the British abandoned which policy of annexation to reassure Indian princes?
solution: The Doctrine of Lapse was given up; princes were assured their territory would not be annexed and were allowed to pass their kingdoms to heirs, including adopted sons.

stem: The 1858 Proclamation of Queen Victoria promised, among other things, to:
options: Respect the rights of Indian princes and not interfere in religious matters
solution: Queen Victoria's Proclamation (1858) pledged to honour the treaties with princes and to respect Indians' religions and customs.

stem: After the revolt, the British reorganised the army by:
options: Reducing the number of European soldiers
Increasing the proportion of European soldiers and recruiting more selectively
solution: The army was restructured with a higher proportion of European troops and recruitment shifted away from regions seen as rebellious, following a 'divide and rule' approach.

stem: The revolt was largely concentrated in which part of India?
options: North and Central India (the Ganga valley and nearby regions)
solution: The uprising was strongest in north and central India (Delhi, Awadh, Kanpur, Jhansi, Bihar), while much of the south, Punjab and Bengal remained largely quiet.

stem: V. D. Savarkar, in his 1909 book, described the events of 1857 as the:
solution: V. D. Savarkar called 1857 the 'First War of Indian Independence' in his 1909 book, challenging the British label 'Sepoy Mutiny'.

stem: One economic grievance behind the revolt was that British policies had ruined many:
options: Artisans and weavers, and burdened peasants with heavy taxes
solution: British manufactured goods ruined Indian artisans/weavers, while heavy land revenue impoverished peasants — feeding widespread discontent.

stem: Indian sepoys had specific grievances such as:
options: Low pay, poor prospects, and being asked to serve overseas against their beliefs
solution: Sepoys resented low pay, limited promotion, racial discrimination, and rules (like overseas service) that clashed with their religious beliefs.

stem: The talukdars and landholders of Awadh joined the revolt largely because:
options: They had lost their estates and power after the British annexation and land settlement
They had no interest in land
solution: After Awadh's annexation, the British dispossessed many talukdars of their estates, so they rallied to the revolt to regain their lost power.

stem: Which Indian ruler is an example of those who helped the British suppress the revolt?
solution: Several rulers, such as the Scindia of Gwalior and the Nizam of Hyderabad, sided with the British and helped suppress the revolt.

stem: The British suppression of the revolt was marked by:
options: Severe reprisals, executions and destruction in rebel areas
solution: The British crushed the revolt with great severity, carrying out harsh reprisals, executions and destruction across the rebel regions.

stem: The son of Begum Hazrat Mahal, proclaimed as the ruler of Awadh during the revolt, was:
solution: Begum Hazrat Mahal proclaimed her young son Birjis Qadr as the ruler of Awadh during the uprising.

stem: The British policy after 1857 of favouring some groups and mistrusting others (especially Muslims, blamed for the revolt) is an example of:
solution: The post-revolt strategy of playing communities and regions against one another is described as a 'divide and rule' policy.

stem: Why did the greased cartridge issue provoke such strong reaction among sepoys?
options: It offended the religious feelings of both Hindu and Muslim soldiers
solution: Biting cartridges greased with cow fat (offending Hindus) and pig fat (offending Muslims) was seen as an attack on the religion of the sepoys.

stem: The revolt of 1857 is significant in Indian history because it:
options: Was the first large-scale, though unsuccessful, challenge to British rule and shaped later nationalism
solution: Though suppressed, 1857 was the first major, widespread challenge to colonial rule and became a source of inspiration for later nationalist movements.

stem: After the revolt, the British increasingly relied on the support of which groups to secure their rule?
options: Loyal princes, big landholders and zamindars
solution: The British cultivated the loyalty of princes and landholders, restoring some privileges to bind them to the colonial order.

stem: Which of the following pairs of leader and centre of revolt is correctly matched?
solution: Rani Lakshmibai led at Jhansi. Nana Saheb was at Kanpur, Begum Hazrat Mahal at Lucknow, and Kunwar Singh in Bihar.

stem: The revolt failed partly because:
options: It lacked unified leadership, common planning and support from all regions and groups
solution: The rebels lacked central coordination, a common goal and nationwide support; many regions and rulers stayed loyal to the British, contributing to its failure.

stem: The last Mughal emperor's role in the revolt shows that rebels sought legitimacy by:
options: Rallying around an old, recognised symbol of authority (the Mughal emperor)
solution: By proclaiming Bahadur Shah Zafar as emperor, the rebels sought to unite under a traditional, widely-recognised symbol of Indian sovereignty.

stem: The Government of India Act 1858 transferred the power of the Company to the Crown and ended the rule of the:
solution: The Act of 1858 abolished the rule of the East India Company and placed India directly under the British Crown.

stem: Which statement about the geographic spread of the revolt is correct?
options: Punjab, Bengal and most of the south remained largely unaffected
The whole of India rose together
solution: The revolt was concentrated in the north-central belt; Punjab, Bengal and most of southern India remained largely calm.

stem: The British removed which symbolic institution as a consequence of the revolt?
solution: With Bahadur Shah Zafar's exile and death, the Mughal dynasty was formally ended by the British after the revolt.

stem: The pension dispute that turned Nana Saheb against the British arose because they:
options: Refused to continue the pension of his adoptive father, the Peshwa
solution: The British refused to pay Nana Saheb the pension that had been granted to his adoptive father, the last Peshwa, angering him.

stem: After 1858, the British promised to respect the religions and customs of Indians mainly to:
options: Prevent another revolt by reassuring the population
solution: To avoid provoking another uprising, the Crown promised religious non-interference and respect for Indian customs.

stem: Which of the following best describes the change in the nature of the revolt after it began?
options: It stayed confined to the army
It spread from the sepoys to involve peasants, artisans, zamindars and ordinary people in many areas
It became a purely religious festival
It turned into a trade dispute
solution: Beginning as a military mutiny, the revolt broadened into a popular uprising drawing in peasants, artisans, talukdars and common people in the affected regions.

stem: The British labelled the events of 1857 the 'Sepoy Mutiny' because they wished to portray it as:
options: A mere revolt of soldiers rather than a widespread popular rebellion
solution: Calling it a 'mutiny' downplayed it as an army revolt, denying its character as a broad-based challenge to colonial rule.

stem: The overall consequence of 1857 for the structure of British rule was that India came under:
options: Direct, more centralised control of the British Crown and Parliament
solution: After 1857, India was governed directly by the British Crown through the Viceroy and the Secretary of State — a more centralised imperial administration.
